DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

The standard reading stands: the “other sheep” of John 10:16 are ethnic outsiders—those not of Israel’s fold—whom the Shepherd must bring into one flock. They are not the scattered Lo-ammi Northern Kingdom under another name.

**The text and the two words the KJV levels.** [L1] John 10:16: “And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” [L2] The Greek does not say “fold” twice. “This fold” is ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης—an αὐλή, a walled enclosure, the sheepfold of John 10:1. The unity promised is μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν—one flock, one shepherd. KJV “one fold” for ποίμνη follows a leveling already in the Vulgate; it is not the Greek. Membership-origin is denied (οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ, “are not of / do not come from”), then a future necessity is asserted (δεῖ με ἀγαγεῖν, “them also I must bring”), then the mark of true sheep is hearing (ἀκούσουσιν; cf. [L1] John 10:27). The saying therefore distinguishes present enclosure from future flock. Unity is by voice and shepherd, not by return to a second Israelite pen.

**“This fold” is the nation in view, not Judah-minus-Ephraim.** [L1] John 10:19, 24: the discourse divides “the Jews,” who demand whether he is the Christ. [L1] John 10:26: “ye are not of my sheep.” The fold in front of the speaker is that covenant enclosure, the nation whose shepherds he has just indicted (John 10:1–13). Nothing in the chapter names Ephraim, Samaria, the ten tribes, or Lo-ammi. [L2] The demonstrative ταύτης points to the enclosure already in the parable, not to a technical “Southern Kingdom.” Narrowing “this fold” to Judah is an importation; the chapter never supplies it.

The Johannine parallel forbids that narrowing. [L1] John 11:50–52: Caiaphas speaks of “the whole nation” (ὅλον τὸ ἔθνος), and the narrator explains that Jesus should die “for that nation; And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.” [L2] οὐχ ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἔθνους μόνον ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα καὶ…συναγάγῃ εἰς ἕν—not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather into one. The high priest does not prophesy for Judah alone. The “only…also” adds a gathering beyond the whole nation. Diaspora members of that nation are still that nation. Children of Israel, northern or southern, are not “beyond the whole nation.” The expansion is past Israel’s ἔθνος, which is what “not of this fold” already said.

**John already has a word for scattered Israel, and a different word for the outsiders.** [L1] John 7:35: “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?” [L2] εἰς τὴν διασπορὰν τῶν Ἑλλήνων…καὶ διδάσκειν τοὺς Ἕλληνας. The Jews themselves separate the διασπορά (scattered Israelites) from the Ἕλληνες (Greeks/Gentiles) whom one might teach. If the other sheep were simply dispersed Israel, John 7:35 has already named them—and distinguished them from the Gentiles. [L1] John 12:20 then brings “certain Greeks” (Ἕλληνες) to Jesus, and [L1] John 12:32 answers: “I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me” (πάντας ἑλκύσω). The narrative sequence is fold of the nation, then Greeks, then a drawing of all. That is the bringing John 10:16 still holds as δεῖ—“I must.” It is not a two-stick reunion scene, which this Gospel never narrates.

**Hearing, not blood, marks the sheep.** [L1] John 1:11–13: he came to “his own,” and his own received him not; those who become sons of God are “born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh.” [L1] John 10:27: “My sheep hear my voice.” [L2] τέκνα θεοῦ in John 1:12 and 11:52 is defined by reception and new birth, not by tribal descent. A genealogical cipher—Lo-ammi Ephraim identified by blood—cannot be the load-bearing identity of sheep whose own book denies blood as the ground of sonship. [L4] The other sheep are therefore outsiders to the enclosure who become children by hearing, not northern Israelites reclassified by pedigree. That inference rests on [L1] John 1:12–13 and John 10:16, 27, and on [L2] οὐκ…ἐξ αἱμάτων set beside οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης: both deny origin-from (blood; this fold) as the ground of belonging.

**The prophetic “also” is Gentiles beside Israel, not Israel beside Judah.** [L1] Isaiah 49:6: it is “a light thing” that the servant raise up “the tribes of Jacob” and restore “the preserved of Israel”; “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles” (גוֹיִם; LXX ἐθνῶν), “my salvation unto the end of the earth.” The tribes are already named in the first charge. The “also” adds the nations. John 10:16’s “them also I must bring” sits on that second charge, not on a renaming of the first. [L1] Isaiah 56:3, 6–7: the “son of the stranger” (בֶּן־הַנֵּכָר / בְּנֵי הַנֵּכָר) who joins himself to the LORD is not to say he is “utterly separated” from the LORD’s people; the house is “an house of prayer for all people” (לְכָל־הָעַמִּים). [L1] Isaiah 56:8: the Lord who gathers “the outcasts of Israel” will yet gather further “beside those that are gathered unto him.” [L2] עוֹד אֲקַבֵּץ עָלָיו לִנְקְבָּצָיו—still/additionally I will gather unto him, to his gathered ones. The additional gathering is coordinated with the foreigner already named in verses 3 and 6, and it is beside the outcasts of Israel, not a synonym for them. [L3] That is the prophetic shape of ἄλλα πρόβατα…οὐκ…ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης: others, not from this enclosure, brought to the one Shepherd. [L4] “Other” here means additional to gathered Israel, hence ethnic outsiders. Footing: [L1] Isaiah 56:6–8 and John 10:16; [L2] נֵכָר / עוֹד אֲקַבֵּץ beside ἄλλα…οὐκ ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης. The chain is: foreigners are expressly joined; a further gathering is promised beside Israel’s outcasts; John’s “other sheep not of this fold” is that further gathering, not the outcasts themselves.

**Lo-ammi does not rescue a Northern-Kingdom identification; the apostle applies it to Gentiles as Gentiles.** The opposing reading must make Hosea’s “not my people” mean the ten tribes, then make those tribes the other sheep. [L1] Hosea 1:9–10: “Ye are not my people” (לֹא עַמִּי), yet they shall be called “the sons of the living God.” [L1] Romans 9:24–26 applies that oracle to “us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles,” and only then quotes Osee. [L2] οὐ μόνον ἐξ Ἰουδαίων ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἐθνῶν—origin from Jews contrasted with origin from the nations. ἔθνη / גוים is the ethnic-outsider term. Paul does not say “not of Judah only, but also of Ephraim.” He keeps the Jew/Gentile distinction in the same sentence in which he spends Lo-ammi. [L1] Romans 9:6–8 has just said the children of the promise are not coextensive with ethnic descent. The Hosea citation widens the call to those ἐξ ἐθνῶν; it does not decode the Gentiles as hidden northern Israelites. If they were already the House of Israel, the contrast “not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles” would be false labeling, and Paul does not write false labels. [L3] Ephesians 2:11–14: those called “Gentiles in the flesh” were “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise,” then made “one new man” and reconciled “unto God in one body.” Strangers from the covenants are not Lo-ammi Israelites temporarily unnamed; Israelites, by Paul’s own list, have the covenants (Romans 9:4). The one flock is Jew plus former alien, which is “one shepherd” over those who were not of this fold.

**The mission horizon matches outsiders, not a second Israelite house Jesus was already among.** [L1] Matthew 15:24: “I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” [L1] Matthew 10:5–6: the present sending is not “into the way of the Gentiles,” but to those lost sheep. That present mission already runs through former northern ground: [L1] Matthew 4:12–15, Galilee of the Gentiles, and the disciples themselves are Galileans ([L1] John 1:43–46; 7:52). Sheep who hear him in that mission are already “my sheep.” John 10:16’s others are still to be brought, and they are not of this fold. They are not the house of Israel under a northern alias. [L1] Matthew 28:19 and [L1] Acts 11:18 name the bringing that follows: “all nations” (πάντα τὰ ἔθνη), and “God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life.” [L2] ἔθνη again—the outsider term, not שבטי ישראל.

**Ezekiel’s one shepherd is real and does not identify these sheep.** [L1] Ezekiel 34:23 and 37:22–24 promise one shepherd and that the two nations shall be “no more two nations.” That restoration stands. It does not gloss John 10:16. In Ezekiel both houses are already the prophet’s two sticks, both addressed as the people being reunited; neither stick is “not of this fold,” an outside enclosure. John never cites the two sticks, never says “Judah and Israel,” and his own book interprets the one gathering as beyond the whole nation (John 11:52) at the arrival of Greeks (John 12:20–32). [L4] Ezekiel supplies shepherd imagery; Johannine context identifies the “other” sheep. That inference does not float: [L1] Ezekiel 37:22 shows what a two-house reunion sounds like when a writer means it; [L1] John 11:51–52 and 12:20 show what John sounds like when he explains gathering into one; [L3] the absence of any Ephraim/Judah formula in John 10, set against the presence of Ἕλληνες in the same Gospel’s gathering texts, keeps the identification on ethnic outsiders. Chain-scope, not a stripped noun: “other sheep” is read inside John’s dispersion/Gentile vocabulary (John 7:35; 10:16; 11:52; 12:20–32), not as an isolated tag for a house John does not name.

The standard reading is the text’s reading. “This fold” is the nation’s enclosure. The other sheep are not from it. John distinguishes their gathering from the diaspora, places Greeks at the hinge, and promises one flock under one shepherd. The Law and the prophets put an “also” of גוים beside restored Israel. The apostle spends the Lo-ammi oracle on those ἐξ ἐθνῶν without erasing the word “Gentiles.” Ethnic outsiders, brought by the Shepherd—not the Northern Kingdom relabeled.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

The standard reading stands: the “other sheep” of John 10:16 are ethnic outsiders—the Gentiles—not the scattered Lo-ammi House of Israel.

**1. The saying, seated in its discourse.** [L1] John 10:16: “And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” [L2] καὶ ἄλλα πρόβατα ἔχω ἃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης· κἀκεῖνα δεῖ με ἀγαγεῖν, καὶ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούσουσιν, καὶ γενήσονται μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν. Two lexical facts control the verse. First, the contrast-term is αὐλή, “enclosure/fold,” and the unity-term is ποίμνη, “flock.” The KJV levels both to “fold”; the Greek does not. He does not promise that the others will enter this αὐλή. He promises one flock and one shepherd. Second, ἄλλα marks other sheep of the same class (sheep), while ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης marks a different enclosure. The distinction is fold-membership, not a second Israelite house hidden inside the word “sheep.”

Who holds “this fold”? [L1] John 10:19-26: the audience is the Jews who have just heard him, and to them he says, “ye are not of my sheep.” [L2] οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν. Presence inside the Jewish enclosure does not make a man his sheep. [L1] John 10:27: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” [L2] The future ἀκούσουσιν of 10:16 is the same verb as the present ἀκούει of 10:27. Sheep-identity in this discourse is voice-hearing and following, not tribal genealogy. [L4] Therefore “other sheep not of this fold” cannot be identified by proving a northern pedigree; they are whoever, outside this enclosure, will hear. That inference rests on the [L1] statements of 10:16 and 10:26-27 and on the [L2] identity of ἀκούσουσιν with ἀκούει.

**2. “Them also” is an addition beyond restoring Israel, and the prophets already named that addition as foreigners.** [L1] Isaiah 49:6: “It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.” [L2] לְאוֹר גּוֹיִם … עַד־קְצֵה הָאָרֶץ. The servant’s charge to raise Jacob’s tribes—and the northern house is among those tribes—is declared too small. The “also” is גּוֹיִם, nations/Gentiles, to the end of the earth. If the “other sheep” were the Lo-ammi north, they would fall inside the assignment Isaiah calls too light, not inside the “also.” [L3] Acts 13:47 quotes this verse as warrant for turning to the Gentiles.

[L1] Isaiah 56:6-8: “the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD… The Lord GOD which gathereth the outcasts of Israel saith, Yet will I gather others to him, beside those that are gathered unto him.” [L2] בְּנֵי הַנֵּכָר are not outcasts of Israel; נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל are. The “others beside” are the sons of the stranger. [L3] John 10:16’s κἀκεῖνα … ἀγαγεῖν (“them also I must bring”) is the same additive structure: a bringing besides the sheep already in this fold. [L4] The prophetic “others beside Israel’s outcasts” are ethnic outsiders; John’s “other sheep not of this fold” takes up that pattern. Footing: [L1] Isa 56:6-8 and John 10:16, [L2] בֶּן־הַנֵּכָר over against נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, [L3] the gather-also parallel.

**3. The Lo-ammi oracle does not identify these sheep as the northern house, because the apostolic writing aims that oracle at Gentiles.** [L1] Hosea 1:9 names Lo-ammi, “not my people,” of the northern kingdom in Hosea’s day. That historical referent is not in dispute. What is in dispute is whether John 10:16 inherits that label as a closed ethnic identity. [L1] Romans 9:24-26: “us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles… As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people… in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people; there shall they be called the children of the living God.” [L2] οὐ μόνον ἐξ Ἰουδαίων ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἐθνῶν, then ὡς καὶ ἐν τῷ Ὡσηὲ λέγει, then τὸν οὐ λαόν μου—the Greek of Lo-ammi. The ὡς clause fastens the Osee citation to a calling that is expressly “also of the Gentiles,” not to a recovery of ten-tribe blood. [L3] Hos 1:10 and 2:23 supply the words Paul re-aims. [L4] A reading that keeps Lo-ammi as the exclusive name of the other sheep must delete Paul’s ὡς. It has no warrant to do so. The chain is [L1] Rom 9:24 plus [L2] οὐ λαόν μου plus [L3] Hos 1:9-10; 2:23.

**4. The bringing is narrated, and the people brought are another nation.** [L1] John 10:16’s δεῖ με ἀγαγεῖν is necessity still ahead of the Jerusalem discourse. Galilee—the old northern territory—has already been his field. [L1] Matthew 4:13-15 seats that ministry in “Galilee of the Gentiles.” [L1] John 4 has already gathered Samaritans, who confess him “Saviour of the world” (4:42). The still-future bring is not those already hearing him in the former north. [L1] John 7:35: the Jews themselves distinguish “the dispersed among the Gentiles” from “teach the Gentiles.” [L2] τὴν διασπορὰν τῶν Ἑλλήνων versus τοὺς Ἕλληνας. # Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** "Biological father" means a male who contributed to the conception of the child. My thesis is that the KJV text gives Christ a mother, Mary, and no human male begetter. Joseph was husband and lawful guardian, not begetter.

## I. The conception stated outright

**1. Matthew 1:18.** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, **before they came together**, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." [L1]
- *Sunelthein* (to come together) is the word for marital union. The text places the conception before it. [L2]
- *En gastri echousa* (having in womb) is the pregnancy. *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of Spirit holy) names its source. The preposition *ek* (out of) states origin. [L2]

**2. Matthew 1:20.** "That which is **conceived** in her is of the Holy Ghost." [L1]
- *Gennēthen* (begotten, conceived) is the verb normally used of a father's begetting, and it is assigned here to *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of Spirit holy). The word that elsewhere names the human father's act names a different source here. [L2]
- The angel gives this to correct Joseph's suspicion in verse 19. Joseph was "minded to put her away privily" because he knew he was not the father. The angel does not tell him he was. [L1] [L4: Matthew 1:19 (Joseph's intent to put her away) + 1:20 (the angel's correction by naming another source) → Joseph's own knowledge and the angel's answer both exclude his paternity.]

## II. The genealogy breaks its own pattern

**3. Matthew 1:2–16.** The list runs "Abraham **begat** Isaac... Jacob **begat** Judas" and so on. Then verse 16 reads: "Jacob begat Joseph **the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus**, who is called Christ." [L1]
- *Egennēsen* (begat) is active, with a male subject, and it repeats for every link. At verse 16 it drops out. The verb becomes the passive *egennēthē* (was born). The relative pronoun *hēs* (of whom) is feminine singular, so it can only refer to Mary. [L2]
- Joseph is called *ton andra Marias* (the husband of Mary). He is not called Jesus's begetter. [L2]

# OPENING — THE DEFENDER

**The question:** Did Christ have a biological father?
**The answer:** **Yes.** The Davidic seed is a flesh seed proceeding out of the body, and the father is named — Joseph — in four independent registers of the text. A man was involved. The record never says Mary had a baby without a man, and it equally forbids narrating *how*. What follows is the text's own rows, quoted, tagged, and joined line upon line.

**THE COLLISION, DECLARED BEFORE THE ARGUMENT:** the trained, pious-sounding default answers this question "no human father." The rows below name a father and require a flesh seed out of loins and bowels. I answer from the rows.

---

## 1. THE SEED IS A FLESH SEED — out of the body, according to the flesh [L1][L2][L3]

[L1] "I will set up thy seed after thee, **which shall proceed out of thy bowels**, and I will establish his kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:12).
[L2] Hebrew *mimme'eykha* — "out of your own insides/bowels"; the seed is anatomical, proceeding from the father's body.
[L3] "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne" (Psalm 132:11); "thy son that shall come forth out of thy loins" (1 Kings 8:19); "of the fruit of his loins, and, **according to the flesh**, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30).

[L1] "Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was **made of the seed of David according to the flesh**" (Romans 1:3).
[L2] *ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka* — *sperma* (G4690) is the begetting-seed word, and *kata sarka* ("according to the flesh") is precisely the biological-origin qualifier Paul adds when flesh lineage is meant. *osphys* (G3751, "loins") at Acts 2:30 is the same word Hebrews 7:5 and 7:10 use of bodily descent from Abraham and Levi.
[L3] "Jesus Christ of the seed of David" (2 Timothy 2:8); "it is **evident** that our Lord sprang out of Juda" (Hebrews 7:14); "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah" (Genesis 49:10).

**Inference [L4], footed on all three:** a seed that proceeds out of bowels and loins, "according to the flesh," and is called *evident* cannot coexist with "no man was involved." [L1: 2 Sam 7:12; Acts 2:30; Heb 7:14] + [L2: *sperma*, *kata sarka*, *osphys*, *mimme'eykha*] → the flesh-seed requirement is stated, not assumed.

**Mary's own mouth [L1]:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48).

**The town [L1]:** "Is not this Joseph's son?" (Luke 4:22); "Jesus, the son of Joseph, **whose father and mother we know**" (John 6:42).
**A disciple [L1]:** "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45).
**The angel [L1]:** "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20); "**THOU** shalt call his name JESUS" (1:21); "and he called his name JESUS" (1:25).

[L3] Convergence: five independent voices name the same man, and the angel's own address — "Joseph, thou son of David" — ties that named father to the Davidic line that Luke 1:27 gives him ("Joseph, of the house of David," *ex oikou David* following *andri ... Iōsēph*). Luke 1:32 gives "the throne of his father David."

[L1] "By the house of their fathers ... every male by their polls" (Numbers 1:2); "they **declared their pedigrees** after their families, by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:18).

[L1] "when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, **made of a woman**" (Galatians 4:4).

## 6. WHAT THE ROWS FORBID — both directions

The text forbids "**no man was involved**" — the seed rows forbid it: out of bowels (2 Samuel 7:12), out of loins, according to the flesh (Acts 2:30; Romans 1:3), and *evident* (Hebrews 7:14). [L1][L2][L3]

The standard reading: Jesus the Christ was conceived by the Holy Ghost, without a human father. This is the testimony of Matthew, Luke, and the prophetic chain beneath them.

## LINK ONE: The text states the conception was of the Holy Ghost, not of a man

[L1] Matthew 1:18 — "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L1] Matthew 1:20 — "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] The operative phrase is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou) — "OF the Holy Spirit," the preposition ἐκ marking source/origin. The Greek is not "influenced by" but "out of, sourced from." Likewise Luke 1:35 — πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπὶ σέ ("the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee") and δύναμις ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει σοι ("the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee") — σκιάζω, "overshadow," the same verb used at the transfiguration cloud (Matthew 17:5) where no human agency is present, only divine glory.
[L1] The negation is explicit: Luke 1:34 — Mary: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω). Mary herself states the absence of the only possible human source, and Gabriel's answer (1:35) supplies the divine source *in place of* it — "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

## LINK TWO: Joseph is expressly excluded as father — he had no relations with Mary until after the birth

[L1] Matthew 1:25 — "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."
[L2] ἐγίνωσκεν αὐτὴν οὐχ ἕως οὗ — the verb γινώσκω here is the Septuagint's euphemism for carnal knowledge (Genesis 4:1 [L1]: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain"). The negated ἕως clause fixes the terminus: no union before the birth. Whatever came after, the conception was patently not Joseph's.
[L1] Matthew 1:19 — Joseph, "not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily" — Joseph's own initial conclusion was that the child was NOT his; his change of mind came only by divine revelation (1:20), not by any claim of paternity.
[L3] Joseph's genealogy (Matthew 1:16) is itself the testimony: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus" — the relative clause ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη ("of whom was born") is feminine singular: Jesus was begotten OF MARY, not of Joseph. The evangelist deliberately bends the genealogy formula — every prior entry says "X begat Y"; at Jesus the chain of ἐγέννησεν breaks.

## LINK THREE: Luke's genealogy and nativity account independently witness the same exclusion

[L1] Luke 3:23 — "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
[L2] ὡς ἐνομίζετο — "as was supposed/assumed." Luke flags Joseph's paternity as legal assumption, not biological fact. The word is νομίζω, "to hold by custom or supposition" — used elsewhere in the NT of what people wrongly assume (Acts 8:35? no — Acts 21:29: "supposed" wrongly).
[L1] Luke 2:5 — Mary is registered "espoused" to Joseph (ἐμνηστευμένῃ) — the betrothal status is maintained even at Bethlehem; the marriage was not yet physically consummated at the census.

[L2] הָעַלְמָה (ha'almah) — with the definite article: "THE virgin," a specific woman known to the sign. The LXX rendered it ἡ παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin") centuries before Christ [L3 — the Greek synagogue text]; Matthew 1:23 [L1] quotes it exactly so: ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει. If the LXX were wrong, the evangelist citing it as fulfilled prophecy would stand corrected; the New Testament underwrites the reading.
[L1] Genesis 3:15 — "her seed" (זַרְעָהּ, zarah): the deliverer is the seed of the WOMAN. In Hebrew lineage reckoning, "seed" is characteristically of the man (Genesis 15:4 — "shall come out of thine own bowels"; 22:18 — "thy seed"). The deliverer is called the woman's seed — an anomaly the standard reading explains: no human sire.
[L1] Jeremiah 31:22 — "the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man" — בָּרָא (bara), the verb of Genesis 1:1, creation ex nihilo, applied to something "new" (חֲדָשָׁה) — a novum in birth.

## LINK FIVE: The doctrinal testimony of the apostolic writers

[L1] Galatians 4:4 — "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman (γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός), made under the law." ## SYNTHESIS

The chain is redundant and convergent: two independent evangelists (Matthew for a Jewish audience via Joseph's legal line; Luke via a Hellenistic-medical investigation, Luke 1:3), one pre-Christian Greek witness (LXX Isaiah), one Hebrew enigma (Genesis 3:15's "her seed"), and the apostolic echo (Galatians 4:4). Each excludes a biological father; each names the source as God. A natural paternity would require the falsity of Matthew 1:18–25, Luke 1:26–38, Luke 3:23's ὡς ἐνομίζετο, Matthew 1:23's citation of Isaiah 7:14, and Galatians 4:4 — that is not one link to break but the whole chain, and the challenger must break them all.

6. THEREFORE Christ had no biological father: He was conceived by the Holy Ghost and born of the virgin Mary — carried by links 1–5.

# OPENING ARGUMENT — DEFENDER

## The Standard Reading: Christ Had No Biological Human Father

The question before this court is direct: *Did Christ have a biological father?* The standard reading of Holy Scripture, from Genesis to Revelation, answers with an unbroken **No**. The conception of Jesus Christ was an act of the Holy Ghost upon the Virgin Mary; no human man supplied seed, no human father contributed to the biological origin of the incarnate Son. I will establish this from the KJV text [L1], the Hebrew and Greek beneath it [L2], and the cross-referencing witness of the canon [L3], building inference [L4] only where two or more prior layers bear the weight.

---

## I. The Explicit Agent of Conception Is the Holy Ghost, Not a Man

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18 states the matter plainly: *"Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."* The phrase "before they came together" (πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτούς) excludes conjugal union before the conception was discovered. The origin is named: **of the Holy Ghost**.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20 reinforces through the angel's word to Joseph: *"Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."*

**[L2]** The Greek of 1:20 is precise: τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ **γεννηθέν** ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου. The participle γεννηθέν is **aorist passive** — "the one having been begotten." The passive voice removes Joseph (or any human male) as the active agent of begetting. The prepositional phrase **ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου** identifies the source (ἐκ + genitive = "out of, from, having its origin in"). The origin is the Holy Spirit. The syntax leaves no room for a second, human source.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35 gives the angel's word to Mary herself: *"The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."*

**[L2]** Two verbs govern this conception: **ἐπελεύσεται** (epeleusetai, "shall come upon") and **ἐπισκιάσει** (episkiasei, "shall overshadow"). The latter is the same verb family used of the Shekinah cloud resting upon the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35 LXX: ἐπεσκίαζεν). The conception is framed as a divine, creative act — not a human biological event. The result clause ("**therefore** also that holy thing… shall be called the Son of God") grounds the divine sonship in the mode of conception itself.

**[L4 — Inference 1]:** The conception of Jesus was an act of the Holy Ghost, with no human male agent. This inference rests on:
- **[L1]** Matt 1:18, 1:20; Luke 1:35 — three separate pericopes stating the Holy Ghost as agent.
- **[L2]** γεννηθέν (aorist passive, agent = Spirit); ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου (source = Spirit); ἐπισκιάσει (divine overshadowing, not human union).

Chain: The KJV text names the Spirit as origin [L1]; the Greek grammar confirms passive conception with the Spirit as sole stated source [L2]. The inference that no human father is present in the biological event follows directly.

---

## II. Joseph's Paternity Is Explicitly Reputational, Not Biological

**[L1]** Luke 3:23 reads: *"And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being **(as was supposed)** the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli."*

**[L2]** The parenthetical **ὡς ἐνομίζετο** (hōs enomizeto) is from νομίζω — to reckon, suppose, hold by custom or law. The imperfect tense indicates a settled public assumption, not a biological fact. Luke, writing under inspiration, **qualifies** Joseph's fatherhood. He does not say "being the son of Joseph." He says "being *as was supposed* the son of Joseph." This is a deliberate, Spirit-guided hedge.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16 breaks the genealogical pattern in a way that is grammatically unmistakable: *"And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."*

**[L2]** Every preceding entry in Matthew's genealogy uses the active verb **ἐγέννησεν** ("X begat Y") with the father as grammatical subject. At verse 16, the pattern shatters. Joseph is identified only as **τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας** ("the husband of Mary"). Then the relative pronoun shifts to **feminine singular**: ἐξ **ἧς** (ex hēs) — "of **whom** [fem.]" — referring to Mary, not Joseph. The verb shifts to **passive**: **ἐγεννήθη** (egennēthē, "was born") rather than the active ἐγέννησεν. Joseph does not beget. Mary is the sole human referent. The grammar itself testifies that the patrilineal chain is broken at this point.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25 adds: *"And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."*

**[L2]** **οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν αὐτήν** — the verb γινώσκω in this idiom denotes sexual knowledge (cf. Gen 4:1 LXX: Ἀδὰμ δὲ **ἔγνω** Εὕαν τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ). The imperfect with οὐκ denotes ongoing abstention through the period before the birth. There was no conjugal union before the birth of Jesus. The biological mechanism of human fatherhood is excluded.

**[L4 — Inference 2]:** Joseph was not the biological father of Jesus; his paternity was legal and reputational only. This inference rests on:
- **[L1]** Luke 3:23 ("as was supposed"); Matt 1:16 (feminine ἧς, passive ἐγεννήθη); Matt 1:25 ("knew her not").
- **[L2]** ὡς ἐνομίζετο (reputational, not ontological); ἐξ ἧς feminine singular (Mary, not Joseph, is the human source); οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν (no sexual union before birth).

Chain: Three KJV passages converge [L1]; the Greek grammar in each confirms that Joseph is excluded from the biological act [L2]. The inference is not speculative but grammatically compelled.

---

## III. The Virgin Birth Is Prophetic, Not Incidental

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: *"Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."*

**[L2]** The Hebrew **עַלְמָה** (almah) denotes a young woman of marriageable age; the LXX renders it **παρθένος** (parthenos), which in Greek specifically denotes a virgin — one who has not known a man. Matthew 1:23 under inspiration adopts the LXX reading: *"Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."* The Greek in Matthew 1:23 is **ἡ παρθένος** — the definite article marking a specific, identified virgin.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:22 explicitly binds the event to the prophecy: *"Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet."* The conception by the Holy Ghost is not an isolated narrative detail; it is the **fulfillment of a prophetic sign** given seven centuries prior. The chain runs: Isaiah's prophecy → Matthew's citation → the event in Mary's womb. Precept upon precept.

**[L1]** Mary's own question in Luke 1:34 confirms her virginity at the moment of the announcement: *"How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"* The present tense **γινώσκω** (I know) indicates her ongoing state. She is, at that moment, a virgin. The angel's answer does not correct her assumption but provides the divine mechanism.

**[L4 — Inference 3]:** The virgin conception was the prophesied mode of the Messiah's entry into flesh, confirming that no human father was involved. This inference rests on:
- **[L1]** Isa 7:14; Matt 1:22-23; Luke 1:34.
- **[L2]** עַלְמָה / παρθένος; ἡ παρθένος with definite article; γινώσκω present tense.
- **[L3]** Matt 1:22 binding the event to Isa 7:14 as fulfillment.

Chain: The Hebrew prophet speaks of a virgin conceiving [L1/L2]; Matthew, writing under the Spirit, identifies the fulfillment [L1/L3]; Mary's own words confirm her virgin state [L1]. Three layers converge.

---

## IV. God, Not a Man, Is Named as Christ's Father

**[L1]** Luke 1:35 concludes the angel's announcement: *"…that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."* The title "Son of God" is grounded in the mode of conception — "therefore also" (διὸ καί).

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: *"But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."*

**[L2]** **γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός** — "having come into being from a woman." The preposition ἐκ with genitive marks origin. Only the woman is named as the human source. There is no "and of a man," no "of the seed of Joseph," no paternal complement. The apostle Paul, summarizing the incarnation in a single phrase, mentions **only the mother**.

**[L3]** 2 Samuel 7:14: *"I will be his father, and he shall be my son."* This Davidic covenant promise, spoken of Solomon typologically, is applied to Christ in Hebrews 1:5: *"For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? and again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?"* The Father-Son relationship is **divine**, not human. God Himself occupies the paternal role.

**[L3]** Hebrews 7:3 describes Melchizedek as **ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος** — "without father, without mother, without descent." While this speaks primarily to the silence of the Genesis record, the language of ἀπάτωρ (fatherless) in the canonical vocabulary is strikingly apt for the One whose true Father is God alone. The type points to the antitype.

**[L4 — Inference 4]:** The paternal identity of Christ is divine, not human; God is His Father. This inference rests on:
- **[L1]** Luke 1:35 ("Son of God"); Gal 4:4 ("made of a woman" — mother only).
- **[L2]** γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (origin from woman alone); διὸ καί (therefore — grounding sonship in conception mode).
- **[L3]** 2 Sam 7:14 → Heb 1:5 (God as Father in the Davidic covenant applied to Christ).

Chain: The KJV names God as Father and Mary as sole human parent [L1]; the Greek confirms mother-only origin [L2]; the Davidic covenant and its Hebrews application confirm divine paternity [L3].

---

## V. The Seed Comes Through the Woman, Not the Man

**[L1]** Genesis 3:15: *"And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."*

**[L2]** **זַרְעָהּ** (zar'ah) — "her seed." The seed is attributed to **the woman**, not to a man. This is the protoevangelium, the first gospel promise. The one who bruises the serpent's head is identified as the woman's seed — a locution that, in a patriarchal genealogical culture, is extraordinary and points forward to a birth without a human father.

**[L3]** Galatians 4:4 echoes this precisely: γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός. The seed promise of Genesis 3:15 finds its fulfillment in the One born of a woman, under the law, with no human father named.

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: *"Made of the seed of David according to the flesh."* The Davidic seed comes "according to the flesh" — through the maternal line (cf. Luke 3:23-38, where the genealogy runs through Heli, understood as Mary's father), not through Joseph's legal line. The flesh comes from the woman. The sonship comes from God.

---

## Summary of the Case

The KJV text, read at the level of its own words [L1], its underlying Hebrew and Greek [L2], and its interlocking cross-references [L3], presents a unified, unbroken testimony:

- The **agent** of conception is the Holy Ghost (Matt 1:18, 1:20; Luke 1:35).
- The **human source** is Mary alone (Matt 1:16, ἐξ ἧς; Gal 4:4, ἐκ γυναικός).
- Joseph's fatherhood is **explicitly qualified** as supposition (Luke 3:23, ὡς ἐνομίζετο).
- The **prophetic sign** required a virgin, not a wife (Isa 7:14; Matt 1:23).
- The **paternal title** belongs to God (Luke 1:35; 2 Sam 7:14; Heb 1:5).
- No verse in Scripture names a human biological father of Jesus. Not one.

Every layer of the text converges. The chain is unbroken.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. **The conception of Jesus was wrought by the Holy Ghost as sole stated agent, with no human male contributing.** Footing: [L1] Matt 1:18, 1:20; Luke 1:35; [L2] γεννηθέν (aor. pass., agent = Spirit), ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου (ἐκ + gen. = source/origin), ἐπισκιάσει (divine overshadowing, not human union).

2. **Joseph's paternity is explicitly reputational, not biological; the grammar of Matt 1:16 breaks the patrilineal chain at Joseph.** Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 ("as was supposed"), Matt 1:16 ("the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus"), Matt 1:25 ("knew her not"); [L2] ὡς ἐνομίζετο (supposition, not ontology), ἐξ ἧς (feminine singular — Mary, not Joseph), οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν αὐτήν (no sexual union before birth).

3. **The virgin conception was prophesied as the sign of Immanuel and fulfilled in Mary, who was a virgin at the announcement.** Footing: [L1] Isa 7:14, Matt 1:22-23, Luke 1:34; [L2] עַלְמָה rendered παρθένος, ἡ παρθένος (def. art.), γινώσκω pres. tense (ongoing virgin state); [L3] Matt 1:22 explicitly binds the event to Isa 7:14 as prophetic fulfillment.

4. **The paternal identity of Christ is divine: God is His Father; the human origin is maternal only.** Footing: [L1] Luke 1:35 ("Son of God"), Gal 4:4 ("made of a woman"); [L2] γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (mother only, no father named), διὸ καί (sonship grounded in conception mode); [L3] 2 Sam 7:14 → Heb 1:5 (God as Father in the Davidic covenant applied to Christ).

5. **Therefore, Christ had no biological human father; His conception was by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary, fulfilling prophecy, with God alone as His Father.** Footing: Carried by links 1–4 above, each resting on two or more prior layers ([L1], [L2], [L3]). The conclusion is the convergence of the chain.

[L2] The Greek behind that English does not repeat one noun. The ὡς ("as") marks the relation as apparent, not actual: compare ὡς in Luke 22:44, "as it had been" — Luke uses ὡς precisely to mark the seeming versus the being. # OPENING: Did Christ have a biological father?

**Position.** No. Jesus had no human biological father. He was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was his father only by legal and reputed standing. By "biological father" I mean a man who contributed to the generation of the child.

## 1. The genealogy changes its verb at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-16 runs on one formula: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob…" Verse 16 then breaks it: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, **of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ**."

**[L2]** The verb throughout is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat, fathered"). In verse 16 the relative pronoun is ἧς (hēs, "of whom"), **feminine singular**. It can only refer to Mary, not to Joseph. The verb becomes the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born"). Joseph is called ἀνήρ (anēr, "husband"), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** From [L1] Matthew 1:16 and [L2] the feminine ἧς, the evangelist who wrote "begat" thirty-nine times withheld it at the one point where it would make Joseph the father. The break is deliberate.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, **before they came together**, she was found with child **of the Holy Ghost**." Verse 20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Luke 1:34-35: "How shall this be, seeing I **know not a man**?" The answer is: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: **therefore also** that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** οὐ γινώσκω (ou ginōskō, "I do not know") uses the biblical idiom for sexual relations. The overshadowing is ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will cast a shadow over"). The causal link is διὸ καί (dio kai, "for which reason also"), so the child's identity as Son of God follows from the manner of conception.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1, "Adam **knew** Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Hebrew יָדַע, yadaʿ, "to know"), fixes the idiom. Mary's question asks how conception could occur without it. The angel does not correct her premise. He supplies a different agent.

# Opening: Did Christ have a biological father?

**Thesis.** No. Jesus Christ had no human biological father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost without any man. Joseph was his father only by legal reckoning, which the text calls "supposed." God is his Father by the Holy Ghost's creative act, not by the ordinary process of generation.

## I. The Holy Ghost, not a man, is the stated source of the conception

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In 1:18 the phrase is *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of Spirit holy." *Ek* means "out of," and it marks source or origin. In 1:20 the participle *gennēthen* ("that which has been begotten") is passive, so Mary is not the begetter. The same phrase, *ek pneumatos*, names the source again. The timing in 1:18, *prin ē sunelthein autous* ("before they came together"), fixes the pregnancy before any union with Joseph.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35 gives the mechanism: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." **[L2]** The verbs are *epeleusetai* ("will come upon") and *episkiasei* ("will overshadow"). Both describe divine action. *Dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the divine act the ground of the title "Son of God." The cause of the title is the conception itself, with no human father in the account.

## II. Mary's own statement excludes a man

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** The Greek is *andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I do not know." **[L3]** *Ginōskō* is the verb of marital knowledge, as in Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife," where Hebrew *yādaʿ* is "knew." The angel does not answer that she will conceive by a man. He answers with the Holy Ghost (1:35). The question and the answer together rule out a human father.

## III. The genealogy breaks its own pattern at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats "begat" for every father: "Abraham begat Isaac... Jacob begat Judas..." Then verse 16 says: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Verses 2–16 use the active *egennēsen*, "begat." Verse 16 switches to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born." The relative pronoun *hēs* ("of whom") is feminine singular. It can refer only to Mary, not to Joseph, who is called *ton andra Marias* ("the husband of Mary"). The chain of "begat" stops at Joseph, and the child is traced to Mary alone.

## IV. Joseph's fatherhood is "supposed"

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Hōs enomizeto* means "as was being reckoned or thought." The verb is *nomizō*, "to think, to hold by custom." Luke himself marks the opinion as an opinion, not as fact.

**[L3]** John 6:42 shows the same pattern in what the crowd says: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" That is popular opinion. Luke 2:48 ("thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing") is Mary speaking of Joseph's legal and household role. Jesus answers at once in 2:49, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" He corrects whom he calls Father.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19–20, 24–25 shows Joseph acting as a husband who is not the father. He is "minded to put her away privily" because she was with child. The angel tells him the child is of the Holy Ghost. Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** *Ouk eginōsken* is an imperfect: "he was not knowing her." It says there was no union in the period up to the birth, which is the period the question concerns.

## V. Prophecy required a woman's seed and a virgin

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Matthew 1:22–23 quotes it as fulfilled.

**[L2]** The Hebrew is *ha-ʿalmāh*, "the young woman of marriageable age, the maiden." The article marks a particular woman. The verse is a "sign" (*ʾôt*, "sign, a marker"), and a sign must be unusual. In Matthew the Greek is *hē parthenos*, "the virgin," which settles the sense for the text we are reading.

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15 speaks of the woman's seed, "her seed," not the man's, which is unusual in a genealogical culture. Jeremiah 31:22 says: "The LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man." Galatians 4:4 says: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." The Greek is *genomenon ek gunaikos*, "come to be out of a woman," with no man named. Hebrews 10:5 adds, "a body hast thou prepared me."

## VI. Joseph's line carried a bar that the legal fatherhood avoids

**[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 says of Coniah (Jechonias): "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." **[L1]** Matthew 1:11–12, 16 lists Jechonias in the line that ends in Joseph.

**[L4]** Chain: if Joseph begat Jesus, Jesus would be "of the seed" of Jechonias (Matt 1:12, 16) and under the bar of Jer 22:30. Yet Luke 1:32 says "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." The throne is inherited by legal descent through Joseph (Matt 1:16, 20, "son of David") and not by blood. Blood descent comes through Mary (Rom 1:3, "of the seed of David according to the flesh"; Luke 3:23–31, the line through Nathan, v.31). The conclusion is that the text's own arrangement makes sense only if Joseph is father by law and not by blood.

# OPENING: Jesus had no human biological father

**Position.** I defend the standard reading. Jesus was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost without a man's seed. Joseph was his legal and reputed father, not the one who begat him. By "biological father" I mean a man who begat the child by his seed. I do not rest on any verse that denies the term in so many words. I rest on the verses that state how the child was conceived.

## 1. The text states the source of the conception

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek is *en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou*. *Gastēr* (G1064) means womb. *Ek* (G1537) means out of, marking source and origin. The source of the pregnancy is the Holy Spirit, and the verse puts it "before they came together."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The Greek is *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou*. *Gennaō* (G1080) here means to be begotten or conceived, and *ek* again names the source. The angel gives this as the reason Joseph should not fear. If Joseph or another man had begotten the child, the explanation would be false.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 both use *ek* for the origin of the child, and both name the Holy Ghost. The text gives the origin of the begetting, and it is not human seed. That shuts out a human begetter.

## 2. Matthew breaks his own begetting formula at the end of the genealogy

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every earlier link uses *egennēsen* (G1080, aorist active), "he begat," with the father as subject. At the end the verb changes to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born." The relative pronoun is *hēs* (G3739), feminine singular, "of whom," and so it points to Mary alone. Joseph is called *ton andra Marias*, "the husband of Mary," and is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." The Greek is *hōs enomizeto*. *Nomizō* (G3543) means to reckon, suppose, or hold by custom. Luke tells us the sonship was reputed, not actual.

**[L4]** Matthew drops "begat" at the one place where Joseph and Jesus meet, and he makes the feminine "of whom" the origin. Luke says "as was supposed" for the same relation. These two lines stand independently, and together they show the son-of-Joseph relation was legal and reputed.

## 3. Mary was a virgin before and through the conception

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097), "I know," is used here of sexual knowledge. The present tense with *ou* describes her standing: she has had no relations with a man.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." *Dio kai* means "for which cause also." The angel's answer to the question "How?" is that God's power will act, not a man.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." Here *eginōsken* (G1097) is again sexual knowledge. Joseph did not know her until the birth, so he did not father the child.

**[L4]** Mary's question in Luke 1:34 and the angel's answer in Luke 1:35 both treat the conception as having no man in it. Matthew 1:25 says the same from Joseph's side.

## 4. The prophecy and the means: "virgin" and "body prepared"

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew is *ʿalmāh* (H5959), a young woman of marriageable age, with *hārāh*, "conceived." Matthew 1:23 renders it with the Greek *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin."

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43 uses *ʿalmāh* of Rebekah, and Genesis 24:16 describes the same Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her." The word is used of a woman who had known no man.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child." The Holy Ghost inspired Matthew to apply the sign to this birth.

**[L3]** Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me." *Katartizō* (G2675) means to fit, equip, or prepare. The body is spoken of as God's preparation.

**[L4]** Isaiah's *ʿalmāh*, Matthew's *parthenos*, and the "body prepared" of Hebrews 10:5 all point the same way. The child's body came by God's working in a virgin, and Joseph did not beget it.

## 5. Anticipated objections

**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "Thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

**[L3]** Luke 3:23 says "as was supposed." Luke 2:33 says "Joseph and his mother marvelled." Joseph was in the household and in common speech the father. John 6:42 shows the crowd's language: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" That records what the crowd said, and Luke 3:23 corrects it with "as was supposed."

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."

**[L2]** The Greek is *genomenon ek gynaikos*, "come to be out of a woman." The text names the woman as the source and names no man, in agreement with Matthew 1:16.

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

**[L3]** Mary's descent is carried through the Davidic line that Luke 3:23 gives, "the son of Heli." Matthew 1:16 says Jesus was born "of whom," meaning Mary. So the Davidic descent comes through the mother and does not require Joseph as the begetter.

# Opening Case: Jesus Had No Human Biological Father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed contributed to the conception. I hold that Jesus had none. His conception was "of the Holy Ghost" in the womb of Mary, who knew no man. Joseph was his legal and supposed father, not his begetter.

---

## 1. Matthew states the source of the conception, and it is not Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The phrase "of the Holy Ghost" is *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537 *ek*, "out of, from as source"; G4151 *pneuma*, spirit; G40 *hagios*, holy). The source of the child is named as the Spirit. "Before they came together" uses *sunerchomai* (G4905, "to come together"), which places the conception before any union with Joseph.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel gives the Holy Ghost as the reason Joseph need not fear. Joseph's worry would make no sense if he were the father.

**[L2]** "Conceived" here is *gennaō* (G1080), "to beget, to bring forth." It is the same verb the genealogy uses for each father in turn ("begat"). Matthew 1:20 assigns the begetting to the Holy Ghost with *ek*, "out of."

**[L4]** The genealogy repeats *gennaō* for every father (Matthew 1:2-16). The same verb in Matthew 1:20 names the Holy Ghost as the source of this child. Matthew therefore replaces a human begetter with another source, and it is not a loose statement about Joseph.

## 2. The genealogy breaks its own pattern at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb changes at the last link. Every earlier link is active, "X begat Y" (*egennēsen*, G1080). Here the verb is passive, "was born" (*egennēthē*, G1080). The relative "of whom" (*hēs*) is feminine singular, so it refers to Mary alone and not to Joseph. Joseph is called "the husband of Mary" (G435 *anēr*, husband, man), not the one who begat.

**[L3]** Compare Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." The pattern of begetting runs unbroken until Joseph.

**[L4]** The pattern is X begat Y. At Joseph it becomes Joseph, husband of Mary, "of whom" (feminine) was born Jesus. The pattern, the shift of voice, and the feminine pronoun together exclude Joseph as begetter.

## 3. Mary's own testimony and the angel's answer

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097). Here it carries the sense of marital intimacy, as in Matthew 1:25. "Man" is *anēr* (G435), a male. Mary says she has not known any male.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982, "to cast a shadow over"). It describes divine power acting, not marital union. "Therefore" is *dio* (G1352, "on which account"), so the angel gives the divine action as the cause of the title "Son of God."

**[L3]** Luke 1:27 first describes Mary as "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." She is called a virgin (G3933 *parthenos*) at the very point of the announcement.

**[L4]** Mary's question assumes that a conception needs a man. The angel does not answer that a man will come. He says the Holy Ghost will come upon her. The answer replaces the human male contribution and does not supplement it.

## 4. The virgin sign

**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L2]** The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin."

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew is *almah* (H5959), which the KJV renders "virgin" here. In Genesis 24:43 the same word names Rebekah: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water."

**[L3]** Genesis 24:16 describes the same Rebekah: "a virgin, neither had any man known her." The word is used elsewhere in the Old Testament for a maiden known to be unknown by any man.

**[L4]** Matthew applies Isaiah 7:14 to the birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:22-23). The Old Testament word *almah* and the New Testament word *parthenos* are rendered "virgin" in the KJV. If Joseph were the biological father, the sign would not be a virgin conceiving.

## 5. Joseph did not know her until after the birth

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** "Knew" is *ginōskō* (G1097), the same verb as in Luke 1:34. "Till" is *heōs* (G2193, "until"), which fixes the abstention up to the birth.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:24 shows Joseph obeying the angel's command: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife."

**[L4]** Joseph took Mary as wife but did not know her until the birth. No marital union therefore stands between the espousal of Matthew 1:18 and the child's conception.

## 6. Joseph is father only by supposition and by law

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** "As was supposed" is *enomizeto* (G3543 *nomizō*, "to think, to suppose, to hold by custom"). Luke marks the sonship as an opinion held by others, not as a fact.

**[L3]** Luke 2:48 and John 6:42 use "father" for Joseph. Luke 2:48 reads: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." John 6:42 reads: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Luke 2:49 gives the answer: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" Jesus corrects the use of "father" in the previous verse by pointing to a different Father. The speakers in John 6:42 are the crowd, who in the same verse are puzzled by "I came down from heaven."

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 labels the sonship as "supposed." Jesus himself in Luke 2:49 redirects the word "father" to his Father in heaven. So "father" for Joseph is a legal and household usage, not a statement of begetting.

## 7. A body prepared and a woman as the source

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

**[L2]** "Made" is *ginomai* (G1096, "to become, to come into being"), and only "a woman" (G1135 *gunē*) is named as the source. No man is named in the verse.

**[L3]** Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me." The body is prepared by God, not produced by a man's seed. Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed," a woman's seed, with no mention of a man's.

**[L4]** Paul gives the entry into the world as "made of a woman" and names God as the one who prepared the body. The two verses together point to a human mother and a divine origin, without a human father.

## 8. Anticipated objection: "seed of David"

**[L1]** Romans 1:3 says of God's Son that he was "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." Acts 2:30 speaks of "the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh."

**[L2]** *Sperma* (G4690, "seed, offspring, descendant") is used here for descent and lineage, not as a statement about the father of this child. Descent can be traced through the mother.

**[L3]** Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." Luke 1:35 follows, and Mary, not Joseph, is the person through whom the Holy Ghost works.

**[L4]** The verses on David's seed state the descent "according to the flesh." They do not say that Joseph's seed was involved. The same Luke that tells us Jesus was "supposed" the son of Joseph also says the child is "of thee," Mary (Luke 1:35).

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** "Biological father" means the male who, by his seed, caused the conception. On the KJV text, Christ was conceived of Mary by the Holy Ghost, and no man begat him. Joseph was his legal and reputed father only.

## 1. Mary was a virgin when she conceived

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."
**[L2]** The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), "a virgin," a woman who has not had sexual relations. Luke applies it to Mary twice in this one verse.

**[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097), "to know," is the verb for sexual knowledge. *andra* (from *anēr*, G435) is "a man." Mary's question is how conception could happen when she has had no relations with any man. Her words rule out a male source before the angel answers.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." Matthew cites this as fulfilled in Mary.
**[L3]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L4]** The prophecy named a virgin, and Luke 1:27 and 1:34 supply her. *Parthenos* (a virgin) and *ginōskō* (know) in Luke 1:34, together with Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in Matthew 1:23, show that the conception occurred with no man involved.

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost, not a man

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** *gennēthen* (G1080, *gennaō*) is "begotten" or "conceived." It is the same root as the "begat" of the genealogy. Where the genealogy names a man as the one who begat, this verse gives *ek pneumatos hagiou* as the source.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L2]** *episkiazō* (G1982), "to overshadow," means to cover with a shadow. It describes divine power at work, not a man's act. *dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the title Son of God follow from this manner of conception.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 give the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*). Luke 1:35 gives the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as the agency, and Luke 1:34 has already excluded a man. The text names one source, and it is not a man.

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
**[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543), "was supposed" or "was reckoned," marks an opinion held by others, not a fact.

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
**[L2]** *genomenon ek gynaikos* (G1096, G1537, G1135) is "become out of a woman." Paul names only the woman as the source.

That is the sense the KJV's "begat" carries in Matthew 1:2-16.

Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac" uses ἐγέννησεν (*egennēsen*, "begat"). Where Matthew supplies a human begetter, he names the father. Where he gives the source of this child, he names ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The Greek διό (*dio*, "wherefore") makes the divine action the stated ground of his being called "the Son of God". The child is "born of thee" (ἐκ σοῦ, *ek sou*, "out of you"). ## 3. Matthew's genealogy withholds the word "begat" at the last link

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 and 1:23 give the reason for the change. The conception is of the Holy Ghost, and the sign is a virgin.

## 5. The Holy Ghost is not a biological father

**[L1]** Luke 24:39: "a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have." **[L2]** πνεῦμα (*pneuma*, "spirit").

**[L3]** John 4:24: "God is a Spirit." Luke 1:35 describes the Holy Ghost "coming upon" and the power "overshadowing", which is the language of divine action, not of natural begetting.

**[L4]** From Luke 24:39 (a spirit has no flesh and bones) and John 4:24 (God is a Spirit), the divine source named in Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 acts as the Creator who causes the conception. It is not a male parent in the biological sense. So the question "biological father?" has no human answer in the record.

**[L2]** The verb behind "begat" is *egennēsen*, from *gennaō* (G1080, to beget). In verse 16 the active verb gives way to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born". The relative pronoun is *hēs*, "of whom", which is feminine singular and so points to Mary alone. Joseph is called *anēr* (G435, husband), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 shows the pattern is "X begat Y". Matthew 1:16 drops that pattern for Joseph and names Mary alone as the one of whom Jesus was born. The author is steering the reader away from reading Joseph as the begetter.

**[L2]** "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982, to cast a shadow over, to envelop). "Therefore" is *dio kai*, "for which reason also".

**[L4]** Matthew 1:20 uses the begetting verb and gives its source as *ek pneumatos hagiou*. Luke 1:35 then ties the child's title "Son of God" to that act with "therefore also". The text puts the Holy Ghost, and no man, in the place of the begetter.

---

## 3. Mary had not been known by a man, and Joseph kept from her until the birth

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph".

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097), used here of marital knowledge. "Man" is *anēr* (G435). Mary's question assumes that without a man's knowing, there would be no conception. Luke 1:35 answers by naming the Holy Ghost instead.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** "Till" is *heōs hou* (G2193 with G3739, until which time). Joseph's not knowing her runs up to the birth.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:18 says she was found with child "before they came together". The conception therefore came before any union with Joseph.

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 shows Mary was not knowing a man. Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 place the conception before, and the non-knowing through to, the birth. The one natural channel of human fatherhood is excluded in the text.

## 4. The sign in Isaiah is of a woman who has not known a man

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water". The Hebrew there is the same word *'almāh*. Genesis 24:16 describes the same woman as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** *'almāh* is used in Genesis 24:43 of a woman Genesis 24:16 states no man had known. The KJV therefore carries the sense of virgin in Isaiah 7:14. A sign that is "a sign" (Isaiah 7:14, "the Lord himself shall give you a sign") is a conception without the ordinary means.

---

## 5. Joseph was only the reputed father

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L2]** "As was supposed" is *enomizeto*, from *nomizō* (G3543, to deem, to hold by custom or opinion). The text itself marks the sonship as an opinion held, not a fact of begetting.

**[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3]** In Luke 2:48 Mary had said, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing". Jesus's reply in the next verse names a different Father.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 gives the reason he stopped: the angel said "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 labels Joseph's fatherhood "supposed". Luke 2:49 shows Jesus himself correcting it. Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph deciding to put Mary away, and he is turned back only by the angel's word in Matthew 1:20, not by his own fatherhood. Joseph's being called "father" is a matter of reputation and household standing, not begetting.

---

## 6. The body was prepared, not begotten by a man

**[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me".

**[L2]** "Prepared" is *katērtisō* (G2675, to fit, to make ready). The body is God's preparing.

**[L3]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Mary is the one who conceives, and the angel names no man as begetter.

**[L4]** Hebrews 10:5 names God as the one who prepared the body. Luke 1:31 names Mary as the one who conceived it. Luke 1:35 names the Holy Ghost as the power that came upon her. Together they leave no place for a human biological father.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. Matthew 1:16 drops the "begat" pattern of Matthew 1:2 for Joseph and says Jesus was "born" "of whom" (feminine *hēs*, G1080 *gennaō* passive). Joseph is called *anēr* (husband), not begetter. [L1 Matthew 1:16; L2 *hēs*/*egennēthē*; L3 Matthew 1:2]

5. Joseph was only the supposed father, and Jesus himself names another Father. [L1 Luke 3:23; L2 *nomizō*; L3 Luke 2:49, Luke 2:48]

# Opening Case: Did Christ Have a Biological Father?

**Position (standard reading):** No. Jesus had a human mother, Mary, and no human biological father. The KJV gives the source of his conception as the Holy Ghost, and it says that Mary knew no man. Joseph was husband to Mary and was only supposed to be the father.

By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed begot the child. I argue in four steps from the KJV text and answer the likely objections in advance.

---

## 1. The source of the conception is named, and it is not a man

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

- **[L2]** "Before they came together" is πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν (prin ē synelthein), "before coming together." The pregnancy is dated before any union of Joseph and Mary.
- **[L2]** "Of the Holy Ghost" is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou). The preposition ἐκ (ek) means "out of," and it marks the source.

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

- **[L2]** "Conceived" translates γεννηθέν (gennēthen), from γεννάω (gennaō, G1080), "to beget or bring into being." The same verb is the one used of each father in the genealogy. Here its source is again ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, "out of the Holy Ghost."

**[L3] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

- **[L2]** "Come upon" is ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai). "Overshadow" is ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei), "to cast a shadow over." "Therefore" is διό (dio), "for which reason." The angel names the cause of the child's being, and no man appears in it.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 each give the source with ek ("out of"). Luke 1:35 gives the means, the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and ties the child's title to it with dio. So the source and cause of the conception is divine. A biological father would be a second human source, and the text names none.

---

## 2. Mary knew no man, and Joseph did not know her through the conception and birth

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name was Mary."

- **[L2]** "Virgin" is παρθένος (parthenos, G3933), used twice in this one verse.

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

- **[L2]** "Know" is γινώσκω (ginōskō, G1097). Here it is used of marital knowledge, and the sense is fixed by the question "How shall this be?" Mary asks how conception can occur, given that she has had no union with a man. "Man" is ἄνδρα (andra), a male.

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:25 show no union of any man with Mary at conception. Luke 1:27 and Matthew 1:23 (with parthenos) show she was a virgin. Isaiah 7:14 shows this is the sign that was foretold. Since Luke 1:35 gives the Holy Ghost as the means, no man's seed is part of the account.

---

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 sets the pattern: "X begat Y" in the active voice. Matthew 1:16 breaks it by changing the verb to the passive and the source to the feminine. A writer who had just said "begat" over and over, and who then declines to say it of Joseph, is excluding Joseph as the begetter.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know"), used of marital knowledge, is negated up to the birth.

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982, "to overshadow") describes a divine act of power, not a marital one. The connective "therefore" (*dio*) makes this act the ground of the title "Son of God".

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."
